# My Inverter Cable Melted While I Was Drying a Dog

**Before I get into this: I’m a mobile dog groomer, not an electrician.** I’m writing down what happened in my van, what an electrician showed me afterward, and the questions I now think every groomer should ask before trusting a van build. Please don’t use my cable sizes or fuse sizes as instructions for your own setup. Your batteries, equipment, cable lengths and loads might be completely different. Get a qualified professional to look at your actual van.

I’m writing this because Tasha is about to put a deposit down with the same person who built mine, and because I know other groomers read this blog. I wish somebody had made me ask these questions before I handed over my money.

On Wednesday, October 28, at about 2:15 p.m., I was in a client’s driveway in Bedford drying Moose, a Bernese mountain dog, on high.

I smelled hot plastic.

My first thought was that something was wrong with the dryer motor. That is where my brain went because the dryer was the thing making noise and doing the work. Then I saw smoke coming out of the bench seat where the batteries are.

I hit the battery switch, got Moose out through the side door while he was still damp, and used the extinguisher briefly. Honestly, I’m still not sure whether I needed to or whether everything had already stopped when I killed the power. There wasn’t some big movie-style wall of flame. There was smoke, a blackened lug, and cable insulation that had melted back about three centimetres.

Moose was absolutely thrilled to be released from his grooming appointment early. He was bouncing around, wet and pleased with himself, while I was trying to figure out whether my entire workplace was about to burn.

Everyone is okay. Moose is okay. I’m okay physically. The van is not.

Moose’s mom brought me a coffee and sat with me on her steps while I shook. I don’t think she said anything particularly profound. She just stayed there, and I will remember that for a very long time.

## What my setup was

The van was built by Coastline Van Fitouts — Darren — in spring 2025. The electrical setup included:

- A **3,000-watt inverter**
- Two **200Ah lithium batteries**
- A **12-volt system**
- **4 AWG cable** on the battery-to-inverter run
- A **300-amp ANL fuse**, mounted approximately **90 centimetres from the battery**

My dryer pulls roughly **1,800–2,000 watts**, depending on how I’m using it. The water heater is another significant load, and sometimes they were operating at the same time.

When I first looked at the van, I thought it looked beautiful. The wiring was neatly routed. Things were secured. There was heat-shrink on the connections. It looked like somebody had taken their time.

That was a big part of why I trusted it.

What I know now is that **tidy is not the same thing as right**.

Priya from Sackville Marine Electric went through the damaged setup with me afterward. I’m going to explain her main points in my own words, because this is the part I wish I had understood before.

## The current on the battery side is much bigger than I realized

I knew my inverter was 3,000 watts. I knew the batteries were 12 volts. I had never properly put those two facts together.

Here is the basic math Priya walked me through. These are rounded numbers to show the scale of the load, not a design calculation for somebody else’s van.

Watts divided by volts gives you amps:

- **1,800W ÷ 12V = 150A**
- **2,000W ÷ 12V = about 167A**
- **3,000W ÷ 12V = 250A**

And those are idealized numbers before accounting for the inverter’s own losses. An inverter is not 100% efficient, so the current drawn from the batteries can be higher than that simple calculation suggests. Battery voltage also doesn’t sit at some magical, unchanging 12.000 volts while you’re using it. If the voltage is lower, the current required for a given output can be higher.

The important thing for me was realizing that I was not asking the battery cables to carry some small, incidental current. Depending on what was running, I could be asking for something in the broad neighbourhood of **150–250 amps**, potentially more under certain conditions.

That is a completely different situation from plugging a phone charger into an inverter.

Priya said that for **my 3,000W inverter on a 12V system, with my installation and intended loads**, the battery-to-inverter wiring should have been **2/0**, not 4 AWG.

Please notice all the qualifiers in that sentence. I am not saying, “Every van needs 2/0,” or “4 AWG always melts.” Cable sizing depends on much more than the number printed on the inverter. The cable length matters. Voltage drop matters. The temperature rating of the insulation matters. The way cables are bundled, routed and ventilated matters. The inverter manufacturer’s instructions matter. The actual loads and how long they run matter.

But in my setup, according to the electrician who inspected the damage, 4 AWG was not adequate.

A 3,000W inverter on a 12V system is a serious high-current installation. The word “12-volt” made it sound small and harmless to me. It isn’t. You cannot judge the demand by the voltage alone.

## The connection under the heat-shrink was bad

The lug on the positive end had not been crimped with a proper crimping tool. Priya said it looked as though it had been crushed with pliers or hit with something like a hammer.

The heat-shrink had been covering it.

I had seen that heat-shrink and taken it as evidence that the connection was professionally finished. In reality, it meant I couldn’t see the quality of the crimp underneath.

A bad crimp can create resistance right at the connection. The plain-language version of what Priya explained is this: when you force a high amount of current through a poor connection, that spot can get extremely hot. It does not necessarily need a dramatic short circuit or more than 300 amps to become dangerous.

That last point matters because the original fuse was rated at 300 amps. It would be easy to assume that, as long as the fuse didn’t blow, everything below 300 amps must be okay.

A fuse is not a temperature sensor.

A connection can overheat because it is loose, damaged or poorly made while the current remains below the fuse’s rating. The fuse can sit there perfectly intact while a lug is cooking.

The visible damage in my van was at that end: the lug was black, and approximately three centimetres of the cable jacket had melted back.

I’m not going to declare one single definitive cause from a blog post. The repair and inspection process are still ongoing. What I can say is that Priya identified an undersized main run for my application, a visibly improper crimp, and protection that was installed much farther from the battery than she said it should have been. Those are facts about what she found, not a theory I invented by looking at photos on the internet.

## The fuse was about 90 cm from the battery

The 300A ANL fuse was approximately **90 centimetres**, or roughly **three feet**, away from the battery.

Priya said the main protection in my installation should have been within approximately **18 centimetres**, or about **seven inches**, of the battery.

The point of placing it close to the source is to limit the amount of conductor that can carry battery fault current before reaching that protection. The wire between the battery and the fuse is not somehow harmless just because a fuse exists farther down the line.

The exact protection requirements and permitted arrangements depend on the system and applicable standards, so this is another thing to get in writing for your particular build. Don’t just measure somebody else’s van and copy the location.

Priya also explained that the type of fuse matters, especially with lithium batteries. The issue is not only the number of amps printed on the front. A protective device needs to be able to deal safely with the fault current the battery bank can deliver.

For my repair, she has quoted a new fuse block and a **Class T fuse**, rather than simply putting another ANL fuse in the same arrangement.

That does **not** mean I’m telling everyone to remove an ANL fuse and buy a Class T fuse this afternoon. The fuse, holder, cable, batteries, inverter and overall layout have to work together. Replacing a fuse with a different type — or a larger rating — without understanding the system could make things worse, not better.

The lesson for me is to ask:

- What is protecting the circuit?
- Where is it?
- Why was that rating chosen?
- What is its interrupt rating?
- Is it appropriate for this battery bank?
- Which part of the cable is still unprotected before it?

I used to think “it has a 300-amp fuse” was a complete answer. It wasn’t.

## There was no smoke detector in the back

The only smoke detector was the one in the cab that came with the van. There was no detector in the rear grooming and battery area.

I can’t say an alarm would have prevented the damage, so I’m not going to claim that. But I smelled hot plastic before I saw smoke, and I initially blamed the dryer. I would like more warning than that in a space where I’m working with a dog, dryer noise, towels, hair and equipment.

Whatever goes back into this van needs detection that is appropriate for the space and installed according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The same goes for the extinguisher: it needs to be suitable, inspected and accessible, not buried under clean towels because that was the only available spot.

If you have combustion appliances, fuel, propane or other equipment, your detection needs may be different again. That’s another professional question, not something to copy from my setup.

## The thermal-camera comparison made my stomach drop

Priya put my damage photos beside thermal-camera images she had taken of her own van operating under a similar kind of load.

Her connections barely got warm.

This was not a perfectly controlled scientific test of two identical vans. But visually, the difference was wild. In her images, the system was doing its job without one connection lighting up as a hot spot. In mine, the discussion was about a black lug and melted insulation.

That was when the whole “but it looked so neat” thing really sank in.

Heat-shrink, cable loom and clean routing can make a build look finished. They do not tell you whether the copper is the right size, whether a lug was properly crimped, whether the fuse is correctly located, or whether a connection is heating up under load.

I bought an inexpensive infrared thermometer for about **$40 at Canadian Tire**. I think every groomer should have one, but I also want to be honest about its limits.

An infrared thermometer reads surface temperature. It can be affected by the surface material and how shiny it is. It cannot certify a crimp hidden beneath heat-shrink. It cannot see a problem developing inside a component. It cannot tell you whether a cable is correctly sized, and there isn’t one universal surface temperature that means every setup is safe.

It is a warning and comparison tool, not an electrical inspection.

Use it only on equipment a professional has confirmed is safe to operate, and don’t start opening covers or experimenting with high loads to “see what happens.” If something smells hot, looks discoloured, is melting or is producing smoke, that is not the moment to take temperature readings. Stop using the system, get yourself and the animals out if it is safe to do so, and call for emergency help if there is smoke or fire.

Please do not run your dryer on high beside a suspect battery connection to test whether it gets hot.

## What you can check in your own van

This is the checklist I’m going to use from now on. Most of it is **documentation and external visual checking**, not electrical work.

### First: make sure it is actually safe

“Turned off at the inverter” does not necessarily mean the battery bank and cables are safe to handle. A 12V system may not present the same shock hazard as household voltage, but a battery bank can still deliver enough current to cause severe arcing, burns and fire if something is shorted.

If you do not know how your system is isolated, don’t guess. Don’t loosen terminals, peel back heat-shrink, open equipment, or stick tools into a battery compartment. Have a qualified person show you the shutdown procedure and inspect the system.

With the system safely off, here is what you can do.

### 1. Photograph every label you can safely see

Take clear photos of:

- The inverter make, model and ratings
- The battery labels and specifications
- The printing along the battery-to-inverter cables
- The fuse type and rating
- The dryer nameplate
- The water-heater nameplate
- Any other substantial appliance that might run at the same time

For the cable, you want the actual printed gauge and specifications, not “it looked pretty thick.”

Check the inverter’s **continuous rating**, not only a big number on the box or an assumed surge rating. Find the manual and look up the manufacturer’s recommended cable and fuse information for your voltage and cable length.

### 2. Write down your real combined load

Do not list only the inverter.

Write down what you actually do during a groom. For me, that means asking whether the dryer and water heater can run together, and what else might be operating at the same time.

Use the appliance ratings to calculate a rough load, then ask a professional to verify the real demand. Add future equipment too. If you plan to install a larger dryer or heater next year, the electrical design needs to account for that now.

Also ask about the batteries’ **BMS continuous discharge limits**. Two batteries having a certain number of amp-hours of stored capacity does not automatically tell you how much current the bank can safely supply. Amp-hours and amps are not interchangeable.

### 3. Trace the battery-to-inverter route visually

Without dismantling anything, note:

- What gauge is printed on the cable?
- How long is the run?
- Is it exposed to high temperatures?
- Is it bundled tightly with other cables?
- Does it pass through metal without proper protection from chafing?
- Is it supported, or can it vibrate and rub?
- Is the jacket cracked, discoloured, swollen or melted?
- Is there corrosion or exposed copper at a visible connection?
- Has anything been rubbing against it during normal driving?

Take dated photographs. If the important portions disappear behind cabinetry, that is a reason for a professional inspection, not a reason to start cutting your van apart.

### 4. Find the main battery fuse and measure its location

Find the fuse holder and read its label. Measure along the cable route from the battery connection to the protective device, rather than guessing based on straight-line distance.

Record:

- Distance from the battery
- Fuse type
- Amp rating
- Any listed interrupt rating
- Make and model of the holder
- Whether there is cable before the fuse that is not otherwise protected

If you have something like my original arrangement — a fuse roughly 90 cm away — ask a qualified electrician to assess it. Do not simply relocate it yourself or assume changing the fuse solves every other issue.

### 5. Ask what is underneath the heat-shrink

You cannot verify the quality of a concealed crimp by admiring the outside.

For a new build, ask for photos of important connections **before** they are covered. Ask what lugs were used and what tool and die were used to crimp them. A proper crimp is not just copper that has been squeezed hard enough to stay attached temporarily.

For an existing van, have a professional inspect suspect connections. Do not slice into heat-shrink or pull on lugs as a DIY test.

### 6. Check alarms, extinguisher access and your exit

Test alarms according to their instructions. Confirm that the detection is appropriate for the area where the batteries and equipment are located, not only the cab.

Check that the extinguisher is the right type, within its inspection requirements, and reachable without climbing over the electrical compartment or a dog crate. Make sure you can get yourself and a dog out without depending on one obstructed doorway.

And if anything has ever smelled scorched, tripped repeatedly, discoloured a connection or melted insulation, stop treating it as a quirk. Get it inspected before using the system again.

### 7. Get somebody independent to inspect it

Ideally, find someone experienced with **high-current DC systems, inverters and lithium battery banks**, not just somebody willing to take a quick look. Priya’s marine background was useful because boats also deal with high-current low-voltage systems, but the important thing is relevant experience and qualifications.

An inspection before a deposit or final payment is a lot cheaper than an inspection after smoke comes out of the bench.

## Tasha, this is the part I need you to read

Before you pay a deposit, please ask the builder — this builder or any builder — for the electrical specifications **in writing**.

You can literally copy and send this:

> Based on my exact appliance list and van layout, what inverter continuous and surge ratings are you designing for? What cable gauge will you use for each battery and inverter run, what are the cable lengths, and what manufacturer information or sizing method are you basing that on? What fuse or breaker type, rating, interrupt rating and location are you specifying? What are the batteries’ BMS continuous discharge limits? What lugs and crimping method will you use, and can I have photos before the connections are covered? Will you provide a wiring diagram and allow an independent qualified electrician to review the design and inspect the work?

A written answer does not guarantee that a build is perfect. But it gives a professional something specific to review, and it gives you something to compare with what was actually installed.

If somebody wants you to rely on “don’t worry, I do these all the time,” that is not a cable size. It is not a fuse specification. It is not a load calculation.

I’m not posting this because I want everyone to demand 2/0 cable regardless of their system. I’m posting it because none of us should be unable to find out what size cable carries one of the largest loads in our workplace.

## Where things stand now

The repair quote is **$4,200** to rewire the main runs, install a new fuse block and move to a Class T fuse arrangement. The estimate is **at least three weeks**, with parts currently on order.

I have cancelled **31 appointments** so far. Insurance’s answer is still essentially “maybe,” and the adjuster is supposed to come Thursday.

Darren has not responded to three texts and an email as of me writing this. I don’t know why, and I’m not going to invent an explanation for him. I’ve included the builder’s name because it is relevant information for people making decisions about their own builds, not because I want anyone to send abuse or start an internet pile-on. If he responds or any of the technical information changes, I’ll update this post.

I am scared. My entire income is that van. Rent is due on the first, and every day it sits there is another day I cannot work. I’m also angry at myself for not asking more questions, although I keep trying to remind myself that customers hire professionals because they are not supposed to have to design the system personally.

Still, I will never again confuse a tidy installation with a verified one.

Moose went home damp and extremely pleased with himself. I got a coffee, a place to sit while I shook, and a much harder lesson than I ever wanted about amps, crimps and fuses.

I’ll post another update when the van is repaired, inspected and back on the road. Until then, if you take only one thing from this: **get the cable sizes, load calculations and fuse specifications for your own setup checked by a qualified professional — and get them in writing before you pay the deposit.**
